events.title: Stockton & Darlington Railway Opens
events.blurb: A steam locomotive hauling 21 coal wagons and one passenger coach completed a 40-kilometre journey through County Durham at a top speed of 24 km/h, carrying 450 passengers on its inaugural run. It was the first railway to carry both freight and fare-paying passengers using steam traction.

events.title: Suez Canal Opens
events.blurb: The French-designed 193-kilometre sea-level canal linking the Mediterranean to the Red Sea — dug largely by corvée (unpaid forced) Egyptian labour over ten years with massive loss of life — opened to international traffic. A procession of 68 ships led by a French imperial yacht sailed from Port Said to the Red Sea over four days. The canal cut the sea route from London to Bombay by about 7,200 kilometres and shifted the geography of global trade.
events.revealBlurb: November 17, 1869 — designer Ferdinand de Lesseps. Giuseppe Verdi's opera Aida, commissioned by Khedive Ismail for the opening, arrived too late and premiered in 1871. The canal was nationalized by Egypt in 1956, triggering the Suez Crisis.

events.title: Homestead Strike
events.blurb: A Pennsylvania steelworkers' strike against wage cuts at a mill owned by a famous industrialist turned into a gun battle after management hired 300 Pinkerton private detectives to escort strike-breakers into the plant. The Pinkertons arrived by barge up the Monongahela River before dawn; strikers and their families met them on the banks with rifles. Nine strikers and seven Pinkertons died in the all-day firefight. The state militia restored order; the union was broken; US steelworkers remained largely non-unionized for 45 years.
events.revealBlurb: July 6, 1892 — Homestead Steel Works, owned by Andrew Carnegie, managed during the strike by Henry Clay Frick. Frick survived an assassination attempt by anarchist Alexander Berkman three weeks later, shot and stabbed multiple times but recovered. Carnegie was in Scotland when the violence occurred.

events.title: Wright Brothers' First Flight
events.blurb: Two American bicycle-shop owners from Dayton, Ohio achieved the first sustained, controlled, powered flight of a heavier-than-air aircraft on a windswept dune at the Outer Banks of North Carolina. The first flight lasted 12 seconds and covered 36 metres — about the wingspan of a modern commercial airliner. They made three more flights that morning; the fourth covered 260 metres in 59 seconds. Few newspapers reported the achievement; commercial aviation took another three decades to arrive.
events.revealBlurb: December 17, 1903 — Orville and Wilbur Wright at Kill Devil Hills, near Kitty Hawk, NC. The flyer is now in the Smithsonian's National Air and Space Museum. The pair spent 4 years after their first flight battling patent disputes and litigation rather than manufacturing planes.

events.title: Ford Model T Goes on Sale
events.blurb: An American automaker released a new car designed to be cheap, simple to drive, and reliable on the rutted rural roads of the era. It sold for $850 — about half the price of the cheapest competitor. Over 19 years of production, the company would build 15 million of them, mostly painted black because that paint dried fastest. At peak production, a completed Model T rolled off the line every 24 seconds.
events.revealBlurb: October 1, 1908 — Ford Motor Company. The 1913-1914 introduction of the moving assembly line cut the Model T's price to $490. Henry Ford doubled the minimum wage at his Highland Park plant to $5 a day in January 1914, partly to cut turnover caused by the line's brutal monotony.

events.title: People's Republic of China Proclaimed
events.blurb: Standing above a vast plaza in the Chinese capital, a revolutionary leader announced the founding of a new communist state after two decades of civil war and foreign occupation. His defeated nationalist rival retreated to an island 160 kilometres off the mainland coast and established a rival regime that persists today.
events.revealBlurb: October 1, 1949 — Mao Zedong declared the PRC from the Tiananmen gate. Chiang Kai-shek fled to Taiwan with 2 million refugees and most of the mainland's gold reserves. The split still defines East Asian geopolitics.

events.title: U-2 Incident
events.blurb: A high-altitude American reconnaissance aircraft was shot down deep inside Soviet territory by a surface-to-air missile. The CIA assumed the pilot was dead and issued a cover story about a weather research flight gone astray. Then Khrushchev triumphantly produced the pilot alive and the wreckage intact, humiliating the U.S. president on the eve of a Paris summit.
events.revealBlurb: May 1, 1960 — pilot Francis Gary Powers ejected over Sverdlovsk (now Yekaterinburg). He was traded two years later for Soviet spy Rudolf Abel on Berlin's Glienicke Bridge — the same swap dramatized in "Bridge of Spies."

events.title: Reykjavik Summit
events.blurb: Meeting for two days in a small wooden house in the Icelandic capital, the American and Soviet leaders came astonishingly close to agreeing to eliminate all nuclear weapons within ten years. The talks collapsed over missile defense, and the two men parted grim-faced. But the intellectual groundwork had been laid for an arms-reduction treaty a year later.
events.revealBlurb: October 11-12, 1986 — Reagan and Gorbachev at Höfði House. The property was reputedly haunted. When talks broke down, Gorbachev said privately: "Can you think of any better way out?" Reagan couldn't, and walked to his car.

events.title: German Reunification
events.blurb: On a crisp autumn evening, a huge black, red, and gold flag was raised in front of the Reichstag building as the East German state ceased to exist and its 16 million citizens became part of the unified federal republic. Forty-five years of partition, imposed by four occupying armies, ended at the stroke of midnight. Crowds sang the national anthem for the first time as one country.
events.revealBlurb: October 3, 1990 — the date is now German Unity Day. The integration cost West Germany over €2 trillion over three decades. Many eastern cities still empty out; many western taxpayers still grumble about the "solidarity surcharge."

events.title: August Coup Against Gorbachev
events.blurb: A committee of Soviet hardliners — the KGB chief, the defense minister, the vice president — placed the reform-minded Soviet leader under house arrest at his Black Sea dacha and announced on state television that he was "unwell." Three days of confusion followed. A reformist Russian president climbed atop a tank outside his parliament and defied the plotters. The coup collapsed in 60 hours, and so, effectively, did the union.
events.revealBlurb: August 19-21, 1991 — the tank-top defier was Boris Yeltsin. Gorbachev returned to Moscow to find his authority gutted; Yeltsin had eclipsed him. Within four months the USSR itself would be gone.

events.title: Rubik's Cube Global Craze
events.blurb: A 3×3 mechanical puzzle cube invented six years earlier by a Hungarian architecture professor became a global bestseller after licensed international distribution began. Over 100 million units sold in the first three years. Books of solutions appeared on bestseller lists. The puzzle's simplicity — six colours, 43 quintillion possible states, a single solved configuration — caught people who had never bought a toy in their lives. World championships began in 1982.
events.revealBlurb: 1981 — Ernő Rubik had patented the cube in 1975; it went international in 1980. The first world championship was in Budapest, June 5, 1982; the current world record for solving it is under 3.05 seconds (Max Park, June 2023). The cube remains in continuous production.

events.title: Compact Disc Launches
events.blurb: Sony and Philips released the Compact Disc — a 12-cm polycarbonate-and-aluminum disc encoding digital audio that could be read by a laser — along with the first commercially available CD players. The digital format eventually killed off the vinyl LP and the cassette, promising perfect sound quality and indestructibility (neither claim quite held up). The first commercial CD, launched in Japan, was Billy Joel's "52nd Street."
events.revealBlurb: October 1, 1982 — Sony, Philips launch the Compact Disc in Japan. European/US launch March 1983. The 74-minute maximum runtime was reportedly chosen to fit Beethoven's 9th Symphony. Over 200 billion CDs have been manufactured.

events.title: Nintendo NES Released in US
events.blurb: A Japanese toy company launched, in a limited New York test market, a home video-game console — two years after it had flopped in its first US release attempt under the brand name Advanced Video System. The relaunched system came with a new console design, a "Zapper" light gun, a robotic companion, and a launch bundle including Super Mario Bros. The North American video game market had collapsed in 1983; the Nintendo relaunch is widely credited with reviving it.
events.revealBlurb: October 18, 1985 — Nintendo Entertainment System (NES). The Japanese original ("Famicom") had launched in July 1983. R.O.B. the robot's inclusion was marketing cleverness to avoid "video game" retailer resistance — the NES was pitched initially as a toy. By 1988, 7 million units had sold.

events.title: O.J. Simpson Verdict
events.blurb: A Los Angeles Superior Court jury, deliberating for only four hours after eleven months of testimony, found a former NFL running back and actor not guilty of the murders of his ex-wife and her friend. The verdict, announced at 10 AM Pacific time, was watched by an estimated 100 million Americans. National productivity visibly dropped during the broadcast. The decision split along racial lines: most white Americans believed him guilty; most Black Americans were skeptical of the Los Angeles police who had arrested him.
events.revealBlurb: October 3, 1995 — O.J. Simpson acquitted. Defense lawyers Johnnie Cochran ("If it doesn't fit, you must acquit") and Robert Shapiro. Simpson was later found liable for the deaths in a 1997 civil trial and ordered to pay $33.5 million. He died of cancer in April 2024 at 76.

events.title: Princess Diana Dies
events.blurb: A 36-year-old former British princess and two others died in a high-speed car crash in an underpass in central Paris after their driver attempted to evade pursuing paparazzi. Her death — ten months after her divorce from the heir to the British throne — triggered a massive public outpouring of grief that caught the British monarchy off guard. Over a million bouquets of flowers were left at London's royal palaces. Her funeral a week later was watched by 2.5 billion people globally.
events.revealBlurb: August 31, 1997 — Diana, Princess of Wales at the Pont de l'Alma tunnel. Her companion Dodi Fayed and the drunk driver Henri Paul also died; bodyguard Trevor Rees-Jones survived. Elton John performed a rewritten "Candle in the Wind" at the funeral, which became the best-selling single of all time.

events.title: First National Film Awards Ceremony
events.blurb: India's first government-adjudicated film awards were presented at Vigyan Bhavan in New Delhi by the President of the Republic, honouring the best films of 1953 across features, documentaries, and children's cinema. The ceremony established that Indian cinema was not merely entertainment but a matter of national cultural policy — a position that has shaped every film ministry since.
events.revealBlurb: October 10, 1954. First Best Feature Film: Shyamchi Aai, a Marathi film about maternal devotion — not a Bombay product, a signal about the awards' intent to honour all Indian languages. The ceremony was conceived explicitly to reward what the state considered the right kind of cinema.

events.title: Pather Panchali Released
events.blurb: A first-time director shot a Bengali village drama across three years in fragments whenever he could afford to — including pawning his wife's jewellery to finish an opening sequence of a boy chasing a train through tall grass. It won a Humanist Prize at Cannes and launched a tradition of realist Indian cinema that bypassed Bombay entirely.
events.revealBlurb: August 26, 1955 — Satyajit Ray's debut. He was a commercial illustrator with no directing experience; the crew were mostly amateurs. The score was composed by an then-obscure sitarist named Ravi Shankar, recorded in a single 11-hour session. The West Bengal government funded its completion after seeing rough footage.

events.title: Bobby Released
events.blurb: A teen romance between a rich Hindu boy and a poor Goan Christian fisherman's daughter — directed by a father launching his second son into stardom — upended Bollywood's existing template of adult romances and star-crossed melodrama. The film's bikini-clad poster and youth-coded aesthetics signalled an entirely new demographic that filmmakers had been ignoring.
events.revealBlurb: September 29, 1973 — Raj Kapoor directing Rishi Kapoor in his leading-role debut, opposite Dimple Kapadia in hers. The film became the highest-grossing of 1973. Raj Kapoor cast Dimple Kapadia after seeing her at a party; she was sixteen. She married Rajesh Khanna five months after filming wrapped.

events.title: Deewaar Released
events.blurb: A story of two brothers who grow up in identical poverty but choose radically different paths — one becomes a dock smuggler, the other a policeman — gave Indian cinema one of its defining confrontation scenes. Its dialogue was so tightly constructed that screenwriters Salim-Javed became as famous as directors, the first time a writing duo achieved superstar status in Bollywood.
events.revealBlurb: January 24, 1975 — directed by Yash Chopra. Amitabh Bachchan's character has "mere paas maa hai" spoken against him, not by him — the misattribution became India's most-repeated film misquote. Director's first choices were Dev Anand and Rajesh Khanna; both were unavailable.

events.title: Dilwale Dulhania Le Jayenge Released
events.blurb: A romance about two Non-Resident Indians falling in love on a Eurorail trip before battling parental disapproval opened in Bombay that autumn and never fully left: it ran continuously at one Mumbai cinema for over two decades, setting a record no Indian film has matched. Its climactic train-platform scene became shorthand for every subsequent Bollywood love story.
events.revealBlurb: October 20, 1995 — Aditya Chopra's directorial debut, age 23. He refused to watch the film with an audience for years. Shah Rukh Khan initially had reservations about the role. The film ran at Mumbai's Maratha Mandir theatre without interruption until 2023 — 1,278 weeks.

events.title: Chauvet Cave Paintings
events.blurb: Deep inside a limestone gorge in southern France, artists of the Upper Paleolithic ventured hundreds of metres into darkness with torches of burning pine and painted more than 400 animals onto the walls — rhinos, horses, cave lions, mammoths — using charcoal and red ochre. The images show sophisticated techniques: perspective, shading, motion. They would remain sealed behind a rockslide until rediscovered by three cavers in 1994.
events.revealBlurb: c. 30,000 BCE — Chauvet-Pont-d'Arc, Ardèche. Radiocarbon dating of the charcoal remains controversial; estimates span 32,000-30,000 BCE. A meticulous replica opened to tourists in 2015; the original site is restricted to scientists to preserve a fragile microclimate.

events.title: Velázquez's Las Meninas
events.blurb: A court painter completed a 3.2-metre oil depicting a 5-year-old Spanish princess surrounded by her ladies-in-waiting, two dwarfs, a dog, and — impossibly — himself at his easel. A distant mirror on the back wall reflects the figures of her parents, the king and queen, who appear to be standing exactly where the viewer stands. The painting is essentially a visual puzzle about who is depicting whom and from where.
events.revealBlurb: 1656 — Diego Velázquez at the Spanish court. The princess is Margarita Teresa. Now in Madrid's Prado. Picasso painted 58 variations on it in 1957. Foucault opened his book The Order of Things with a long reading of its perspective.

events.title: First Impressionist Exhibition
events.blurb: Thirty painters whose work had been repeatedly rejected by the official French Salon rented the studio of a photographer on a Paris boulevard and held their own group show. A review in a satirical magazine mocked one of the paintings — "Impression, Sunrise" — and gave the movement the name it would keep. The show attracted 3,500 visitors, which was dismal; mockery outweighed admiration; most of the painters struggled financially for another decade.
events.revealBlurb: April 15 to May 15, 1874 — 35 Boulevard des Capucines, Paris. Participants included Monet, Renoir, Degas, Pissarro, Cézanne, Berthe Morisot, and Sisley. The critic who coined the term, Louis Leroy, titled his review "Exhibition of the Impressionists" sarcastically; the painters adopted it.

events.title: Van Gogh Paints The Starry Night
events.blurb: A 36-year-old Dutch painter, voluntarily committed to a mental asylum in a Provençal town, painted from memory — and through the bars of his east-facing window — a night sky filled with swirling nebulae and stars dozens of times their actual size, above a village with an exaggeratedly prominent church steeple. He considered the painting a failure. It is now among the most recognized images in Western art.
events.revealBlurb: June 1889 — Saint-Paul-de-Mausole asylum, Saint-Rémy-de-Provence. The village in the picture does not match the actual view. The Museum of Modern Art in New York has owned it since 1941. Recent research suggests the sky's swirls resemble actual fluid turbulence.

events.title: Banksy Shreds at Auction
events.blurb: A framed spray-painting of a girl releasing a heart-shaped balloon, sold at a London auction for £1.04 million ten seconds earlier, began to buzz mechanically and slid partway through a concealed shredder built into the custom frame. Half the canvas emerged in vertical strips; the auction house staff stared; the hammer had already fallen. The anonymous street artist who had built the device posted a video saying the mechanism was supposed to shred the whole picture.
events.revealBlurb: October 5, 2018 — Banksy, at Sotheby's London. The buyer honored the purchase. The half-shredded work was retitled "Love is in the Bin" and resold three years later for £18.6 million — 18 times the original price.

events.title: The Jazz Singer Released
events.blurb: A Warner Brothers feature film about a cantor's son who runs away to become a vaudeville singer premiered at a Times Square theatre as the first full-length motion picture with synchronized recorded dialogue. The star, in blackface for most of the film, delivered the industry's first-ever spoken movie line: "Wait a minute, wait a minute. You ain't heard nothin' yet!" Within three years almost every Hollywood film was a talkie.
events.revealBlurb: October 6, 1927 — Al Jolson at the Warners' Theatre, NYC. The film's sound system, Vitaphone, used synchronized phonograph records rather than optical audio. The silent era ended astonishingly fast; by 1930 the major Hollywood studios had written off the previous decade's technology.

events.title: Bicycle Thieves Released
events.blurb: An Italian director released a quiet 89-minute film about an unemployed working-class man whose stolen bicycle means he cannot take a new job pasting posters on walls. The non-professional actors, documentary-style camera, and refusal of melodramatic conventions defined the Italian neorealist movement. The film spoke for a generation of post-war European audiences who had had enough of Hollywood glamour.
events.revealBlurb: November 24, 1948 — Vittorio De Sica. The father was played by a real factory worker; the son by a young boy De Sica spotted on the street. It won an honorary Academy Award before the foreign language category existed. Its influence on later directors — from Ken Loach to Satyajit Ray — is enormous.

events.title: Rashomon Released
events.blurb: A 40-year-old Japanese director released a 88-minute film in which the same violent encounter is recounted by four different participants, none of whom agrees with any of the others. The Venice Film Festival awarded it the Golden Lion the following year, and the world film industry discovered Japanese cinema as a major force. The very title became an English noun: "the Rashomon effect" is the concept of contradictory memories.
events.revealBlurb: August 26, 1950 — Akira Kurosawa. The producers were reportedly baffled by the script and wanted it re-edited. Its Venice win completely blindsided Japanese critics, who had not thought much of the film. It led directly to the global reception of Ozu, Mizoguchi, and Kurosawa's later work.

events.title: E.T. the Extra-Terrestrial Released
events.blurb: A 35-year-old American director released a 115-minute family film about a stranded alien befriended by a suburban boy who helps him contact his home planet. The director had developed the story as a way of processing his parents' divorce and his imaginary childhood companion. The film topped the box office for 16 weeks, displaced Star Wars as the highest-grossing film of all time, and moved children to tears for decades.
events.revealBlurb: June 11, 1982 — Steven Spielberg. Composer John Williams won the Oscar for his score; Spielberg himself didn't. The flying-bicycle silhouette against the moon became the logo of Amblin Entertainment, his production company.

events.title: Jurassic Park Released
events.blurb: A 46-year-old director released an adaptation of a recent Michael Crichton novel about genetically resurrected dinosaurs on a tropical-island theme park. The film's digital dinosaurs — only a few minutes of CGI, mixed with extensive full-size animatronic puppets — changed the calculus of what visual effects could do. Audiences gasped at a Tyrannosaurus rex roaring over a rain-soaked jeep; a decade of purely physical-effects films were obsolete.
events.revealBlurb: June 11, 1993 — Steven Spielberg. The T. rex breaking into the jeep was actually animatronic; it malfunctioned often in the Hawaii humidity. The film displaced E.T. as highest-grossing ever. Spielberg was editing "Schindler's List" at night during production.

events.title: Charlemagne Crowned Emperor
events.blurb: A Frankish king, in a papal basilica in the old western imperial capital for Christmas Mass, rose from prayer to be unexpectedly crowned "Emperor of the Romans" by the pope. The coronation resurrected, at least in title, a western empire that had been extinct for 324 years, and established a relationship between popes and emperors that would shape European politics for eight centuries.
events.revealBlurb: December 25, 800 — Charlemagne in Rome, crowned by Pope Leo III. Charlemagne later claimed he had been surprised — but the pope probably wouldn't have dared without his consent. The Holy Roman Empire survived in one form or another until 1806.

events.title: Battle of Hastings
events.blurb: A Norman duke from across the English Channel invaded a southern English kingdom with 7,000 men, met its exhausted king — who had marched south after defeating a Norwegian invasion three weeks earlier in the north — on a hillside near the coast, and won in an all-day battle. The English king was killed, reportedly by an arrow through the eye. The victor replaced the Anglo-Saxon aristocracy with his own.
events.revealBlurb: October 14, 1066 — William the Conqueror vs. Harold Godwinson near the town of Battle, East Sussex. The Bayeux Tapestry, a 70-metre embroidered account, was sewn within a decade. Modern English is still 50–60 percent French-derived because of the resulting Norman elite.

events.title: First Crusade Takes Jerusalem
events.blurb: After a month-long siege and a three-year, 3,000-kilometre march from Europe, an army of Frankish knights and footsoldiers breached the walls of a holy city in the Levant and slaughtered its Muslim and Jewish inhabitants indiscriminately over two days — perhaps 30,000 people. The first crusader state was established with a European dynasty on the throne; it would last 88 years.
events.revealBlurb: July 15, 1099 — the siege was broken when two Flemish knights scaled a siege tower onto the wall. The leaders competed to be the first to reach the Holy Sepulchre. Godfrey of Bouillon refused the crown of a city "where his savior had worn a crown of thorns" — he was titled "Defender" instead.

events.title: Black Death Reaches Europe
events.blurb: A plague arriving by trade galley at a Sicilian port spread through Mediterranean shipping lanes and overland caravans until, over the next five years, it killed an estimated 30-60 percent of Europe's population — perhaps 50 million people. Physicians had no effective response; flagellant processions and mass pogroms of Jews did little but spread the disease faster.
events.revealBlurb: October 1347 — Messina, Sicily. Caused by Yersinia pestis, spread by the fleas of black rats. Wages for surviving laborers roughly doubled; labor scarcity began eroding feudal obligations. The plague cycled back every decade or so for the next three centuries.

events.title: Siege of Orléans Lifted
events.blurb: A 17-year-old peasant girl from Lorraine, dressed in white armour and claiming visions from saints, led a French relief army into a besieged Loire Valley city. Over eight days of sorties, she personally led assaults on the English siege forts around the city, was shot through the shoulder with a crossbow bolt, returned to the fight, and broke the siege. The French war effort, exhausted for a generation, was transformed overnight.
events.revealBlurb: May 8, 1429 — Joan of Arc relieves Orléans. She had convinced a skeptical Dauphin to give her an army by passing a theological interrogation and, reportedly, a virginity test. She would see him crowned as Charles VII at Reims within ten weeks.

events.title: Great Chicago Fire
events.blurb: A fire started in a barn on a windy autumn evening in the second-largest U.S. metropolis and burned for 27 hours, destroying 17,500 buildings across 8.5 square kilometres of the central business district and killing around 300 people. A third of the city's population was left homeless.
events.revealBlurb: October 8-10, 1871 — Chicago. The Mrs. O'Leary's cow story is almost certainly a fabrication invented by a reporter who later confessed. On the very same day, the deadlier Peshtigo fire in Wisconsin killed 1,500+ people but is largely forgotten.

events.title: 1931 China Floods
events.blurb: A succession of heavy snowmelt and monsoon rains caused the three great rivers of central China to breach their banks simultaneously, flooding 180,000 square kilometres of farmland and cities. Estimates of the death toll range from 500,000 to 4 million; much of the toll came from subsequent famine and water-borne disease. It is likely the deadliest non-pandemic natural disaster in recorded history.
events.revealBlurb: July-November 1931 — Yangtze, Yellow, and Huai rivers. Wuhan was submerged for months. A young Chiang Kai-shek's Nationalist government was blamed for the weak response; flood relief was a major propaganda opportunity for the Communists in Jiangxi.

events.title: Hindenburg Disaster
events.blurb: A German passenger airship, the largest aircraft ever flown, caught fire as it approached its mooring mast at a New Jersey naval air station, and was consumed in less than 40 seconds. 36 of the 97 people on board died, along with one ground crew member. A radio reporter's anguished live commentary — "Oh, the humanity!" — entered popular idiom.
events.revealBlurb: May 6, 1937 — Lakehurst, NJ. The reporter was Herbert Morrison; he was actually there to record for later broadcast and didn't expect to be on air. The disaster effectively killed the commercial airship industry overnight.

events.title: Tōhoku Earthquake & Fukushima
events.blurb: A magnitude 9.1 undersea earthquake off the Pacific coast of northern Japan triggered tsunami waves up to 40 metres high that killed some 19,700 people and swamped the seawalls of a coastal nuclear plant. Three reactor cores melted down in the following days, contaminating 337 square kilometres of surrounding countryside. 165,000 people were displaced; many never returned.
events.revealBlurb: March 11, 2011 — 2:46 PM local time. The quake was so powerful it shifted Earth's axis by about 17 centimetres and shortened the day by 1.8 microseconds. The plant's operator, TEPCO, had been warned about tsunami risk years earlier and ignored it.

events.title: Turkey-Syria Earthquake
events.blurb: A magnitude 7.8 earthquake struck in the pre-dawn darkness along the fault separating the Anatolian and Arabian tectonic plates, followed nine hours later by a nearly equal-magnitude aftershock. Over 59,000 people died across southern Turkey and northern Syria; 1.5 million were left homeless. Shoddy building construction, exempted from code over years of amnesty laws, drew furious public blame.
events.revealBlurb: February 6, 2023 — epicenter near Gaziantep. The disaster reshaped the Turkish elections three months later; contractors who had benefited from construction amnesties were prosecuted. In Syria, ongoing civil war hampered aid delivery.

events.title: Partition of Bengal
events.blurb: A British viceroy, citing administrative efficiency, split a vast eastern province of colonial India into two along religious lines — a Muslim-majority east and a Hindu-majority west — over the fierce protests of its Bengali elite. Boycotts of British goods, the Swadeshi movement, and targeted assassinations followed. The partition was reversed six years later, but the communal logic it had introduced could not be uninvented.
events.revealBlurb: October 16, 1905 — announced by Lord Curzon. Rabindranath Tagore led Hindus and Muslims in tying rakhis on each other's wrists in protest. The reunification in 1911 coincided with moving the colonial capital from Calcutta to Delhi.

events.title: Jallianwala Bagh Massacre
events.blurb: A British brigadier-general marched 50 rifle-armed soldiers into a walled garden in a Punjabi city where thousands of Sikhs, Hindus, and Muslims had gathered for a spring harvest festival. Without warning, he ordered ten minutes of continuous fire into the unarmed crowd, ceasing only when ammunition ran low. Official counts put the dead at 379; Indian sources gave over 1,000. He was celebrated in parts of British society as a saviour of empire.
events.revealBlurb: April 13, 1919 — Amritsar, Baisakhi day. Brigadier-General Reginald Dyer. The poet Rabindranath Tagore renounced his British knighthood in protest. A young Sikh named Udham Singh, who was at the garden that day, assassinated the former lieutenant-governor responsible for the region 21 years later in London.

events.title: Bhagat Singh Executed
events.blurb: Three young revolutionaries were hanged an hour earlier than scheduled at a jail in a Punjabi city, after a three-year trial for killing a British police officer they had mistaken for the superintendent they had meant to assassinate. The youngest of them was 23. Crowds had gathered outside the prison expecting the normal morning execution time; by the time they arrived, the bodies had already been smuggled out and cremated by the riverside.
events.revealBlurb: March 23, 1931 — Bhagat Singh, Rajguru, and Sukhdev at Lahore Central Jail. Their martyrdom made them arguably the most venerated revolutionaries of the independence movement, an icon Gandhi's non-violent path never quite matched among the young.

events.title: Indian Independence & Partition
events.blurb: At the stroke of midnight, two new independent dominions came into existence on the subcontinent — one majority-Hindu, one majority-Muslim — as the British flag was lowered on the largest and oldest of Britain's imperial possessions. The division of provinces along religious lines displaced between 10 and 20 million people, and perhaps a million died in the communal violence that followed.
events.revealBlurb: August 14-15, 1947 — Pakistan on the 14th, India on the 15th. The boundary lines had been drawn by a London barrister, Cyril Radcliffe, who had never visited the subcontinent and had 36 days to complete the task. Nehru's "Tryst with Destiny" speech was delivered at midnight from the Constituent Assembly.

events.title: Right to Information Act
events.blurb: A law guaranteeing any citizen of the country the right to request information from public authorities — and compelling officials to respond within 30 days or face personal penalties — came into force after a decade-long campaign driven by rural social movements in a western state. It quickly became one of the most-used such laws in the world, exposing corruption from village panchayats to the prime minister's office.
events.revealBlurb: October 12, 2005 — RTI Act. Aruna Roy's Mazdoor Kisan Shakti Sangathan was the movement's backbone. Its origins lay in drought-era sit-ins demanding to see the village wage registers. More than a hundred RTI activists have been murdered since passage.

events.title: Universal Declaration of Human Rights
events.blurb: The United Nations General Assembly, meeting in a Paris exhibition hall, adopted a declaration of 30 articles enumerating rights that every human being was to be considered entitled to by virtue of humanity itself. The document's drafting committee, chaired by the widow of a U.S. president, had spent two years negotiating across ideological and cultural lines. No state voted against; eight abstained.
events.revealBlurb: December 10, 1948 — Eleanor Roosevelt chaired the drafting committee. Adopted 48-0 with 8 abstentions (Soviet bloc, Saudi Arabia, South Africa). Translated into over 500 languages — more than any other document. December 10 is now International Human Rights Day.

events.title: Margaret Thatcher Becomes PM
events.blurb: The leader of the British Conservative Party, a grocer's daughter who had studied chemistry at Oxford and later trained as a barrister, was invited by the monarch to form a government after her party won a sweeping parliamentary majority. She became the United Kingdom's first woman prime minister and would hold the office for 11 years — the longest continuous premiership of the 20th century.
events.revealBlurb: May 4, 1979 — she took office quoting St. Francis of Assisi on the doorstep: "Where there is discord, may we bring harmony." The next decade would be anything but that. She was forced to resign by her own cabinet in November 1990.

events.title: Sandra Day O'Connor Confirmed
events.blurb: A 51-year-old former state senator and state appellate judge from the American Southwest was confirmed by the U.S. Senate 99-0 as the first woman to sit on the U.S. Supreme Court, fulfilling a campaign promise the president who had nominated her made during the 1980 election. She would serve 24 years, writing decisions on affirmative action, abortion, and the disputed 2000 election.
events.revealBlurb: September 21, 1981 — confirmed; Ronald Reagan had nominated her. Her 2005 retirement was precipitated by her husband's declining health from Alzheimer's. She herself was diagnosed with dementia in 2018 and died in 2023.

events.title: Malala Yousafzai Wins Nobel
events.blurb: A 17-year-old Pakistani girl, who had been shot in the head by a Taliban gunman on her school bus two years earlier for publicly advocating for girls' education, became the youngest-ever winner of the world's most prestigious peace prize. She shared the award with an Indian child-rights activist. She had been giving anonymous interviews to the BBC since age 11; she was now a household name.
events.revealBlurb: October 10, 2014 — Malala Yousafzai and Kailash Satyarthi. She was attacked on October 9, 2012 in Swat Valley and underwent multiple surgeries in the UK. Her autobiography had been published the previous year. She was 11 years below the previous youngest laureate.

events.title: #MeToo Goes Viral
events.blurb: Five days after a major U.S. newspaper published a long investigation into sexual harassment and assault allegations against a powerful Hollywood film producer, an actress posted on Twitter asking women who had been sexually harassed or assaulted to reply with two words. Within 24 hours, those two words had been used 500,000 times on Twitter alone. The phrase had been coined a decade earlier by a Black activist working with survivors in the American South.
events.revealBlurb: October 15, 2017 — Alyssa Milano's tweet; the phrase was coined in 2006 by Tarana Burke. The producer was Harvey Weinstein, finally convicted of rape in February 2020. A cascade of resignations, prosecutions, and cultural reckoning followed across industries.

events.title: One Thousand and One Nights Compiled
events.blurb: An anonymous Arabic compiler assembled a frame narrative and embedded stories drawn from Persian, Indian, Mesopotamian, and Egyptian sources into a single cycle. The outer frame told of a queen stalling her own execution by telling her king a new story every night; the inner tales — of flying carpets, genies, thieves — became permanent fixtures of world storytelling. The collection continued to accrete new tales for centuries.
events.revealBlurb: c. 10th century CE — the oldest surviving Arabic manuscript dates from the 14th century. "Aladdin," "Ali Baba," and "Sinbad" were added to the collection by an 18th-century French translator, Antoine Galland, working from Syrian oral sources. They are not in the original Arabic canon.

events.title: Johnson's Dictionary Published
events.blurb: An Oxford-educated English essayist, working nine years with six assistants in a garret flat, completed and published a two-volume dictionary of the English language — the first comprehensive, systematically illustrated dictionary of the vernacular. It defined 42,773 words with 114,000 quotations showing their use. It was the standard English dictionary until Oxford's larger project finally superseded it 173 years later.
events.revealBlurb: April 15, 1755 — Samuel Johnson. He defined "lexicographer" as "a harmless drudge, that busies himself in tracing the original, and detailing the signification of words." His tart definitions became famous in their own right: "Oats: A grain, which in England is generally given to horses, but in Scotland supports the people."

events.title: Moby-Dick Published
events.blurb: A 31-year-old American novelist published his sixth novel — a 135-chapter whaling yarn interleaved with encyclopedic digressions on cetacean anatomy, metaphysical speculation, and a revenge monomania culminating in an apocalyptic confrontation with a great white whale. The book sold 3,215 copies in its first 18 months and then essentially nothing for decades. The author died largely forgotten. The rediscovery of the novel's greatness did not come until the 1920s.
events.revealBlurb: October 18, 1851 — Herman Melville. The white whale was loosely based on a real albino sperm whale, Mocha Dick, which reportedly stove in ships. The book was first published in London as "The Whale"; the American edition restored the title "Moby-Dick; or, The Whale."

events.title: Ulysses Published
events.blurb: An English-language bookshop owner in Paris published a 730-page Irish novel by a 40-year-old expatriate author that had been serialized, banned, confiscated, and partially burned in the United States. The book followed a single day — June 16, 1904 — in the lives of two Dublin men, using stream-of-consciousness narration that shifted style dozens of times across its 18 chapters. The American mail service seized copies until 1934.
events.revealBlurb: February 2, 1922 — James Joyce, 40th birthday; published by Sylvia Beach at Shakespeare and Company, Paris. The setting day — known as "Bloomsday" — is celebrated by Joyceans every June 16 with readings, pub crawls, and costumed reenactments.

events.title: To Kill a Mockingbird Published
events.blurb: A 34-year-old Alabama-born New York airline reservation clerk published her first and, for over half a century, only novel — a semi-autobiographical story narrated by a six-year-old white girl whose father, a small-town Southern lawyer, defends a Black man falsely accused of raping a white woman. The book won a Pulitzer the next year and has been a school-curriculum fixture in the U.S. ever since.
events.revealBlurb: July 11, 1960 — Harper Lee. Her childhood friend Truman Capote was the model for the character Dill. Gregory Peck won an Oscar for the film adaptation. Lee published a second novel, "Go Set a Watchman," in 2015, a year before her death; it was an earlier draft of the same book.

events.title: Columbus Makes Landfall
events.blurb: A Genoese navigator commanding three vessels landed on an island in the present-day Bahamas after 70 days at sea, believing he had reached islands off the coast of Asia. He planted a royal standard, claimed the land in the name of the Spanish Crown, and named the island San Salvador — its indigenous inhabitants called it Guanahani.

events.title: Galileo's Telescope Observations
events.blurb: A 46-year-old Paduan university mathematics professor, having improved the magnification of a newly invented Dutch optical toy from 3x to 30x, pointed his telescope at the night sky. Over the following months he observed craters on the moon, four previously unknown moons circling Jupiter, phases of Venus, and individual stars resolvable in the milky white band of the Milky Way. His findings, published in a short Latin book, transformed astronomy.
events.revealBlurb: January 7, 1610 — Galileo Galilei observed Jupiter's moons from Padua. His book "Sidereus Nuncius" (The Starry Messenger) was rushed into print in March. The phases of Venus, observed later that year, were decisive evidence against the Ptolemaic earth-centered model.

events.title: King James Bible Published
events.blurb: An English translation committee of 47 scholars, working in six sub-committees across three cathedrals, completed a new authorized English Bible commissioned seven years earlier by the English king at a church conference. Rather than abandon earlier translations, they drew liberally on William Tyndale's sixteenth-century Protestant version. The resulting text shaped English-language literary style so pervasively that its phrases are still in routine use four centuries later.
events.revealBlurb: 1611 — commissioned at the Hampton Court Conference, 1604. James I of England (and VI of Scotland) authorized it. Its prose cadences, largely inherited from Tyndale, influenced Shakespeare, Milton, Blake, Dickens, and Lincoln. Its Old Testament translation was done primarily at Westminster and Cambridge; the New at Oxford.

events.title: Mayflower Compact Signed
events.blurb: 41 male passengers of a merchant ship that had landed at the wrong spot on the Massachusetts coast — they had intended the Hudson River — signed a short agreement on the ship to govern themselves by the will of the majority until permanent civil authority could be established. The document was pragmatic, not ideological, but became a foundational text of American self-government. The Pilgrims who signed it were fleeing religious persecution in England via the Netherlands.
events.revealBlurb: November 11, 1620 (Old Style) / November 21, 1620 (New Style) — aboard the Mayflower, Cape Cod. Half the colony's 102 passengers died of scurvy and starvation the first winter. The autumn 1621 harvest feast with the Wampanoag is the ancestor of the American Thanksgiving.

events.title: Bacon's Novum Organum
events.blurb: A 59-year-old English Lord Chancellor published a Latin treatise proposing a new method for the natural sciences — not the deduction from first principles that Aristotelian scholars had relied on for eighteen centuries, but the patient inductive accumulation of observations, cataloguing of anomalies, and testing of hypotheses. The method he described, refined and formalized over the next century, became recognizable as the modern scientific method.
events.revealBlurb: 1620 — Francis Bacon, "Novum Organum Scientiarum." He was dismissed from the Lord Chancellorship the next year for taking bribes. He died in 1626 after catching pneumonia from stuffing a chicken with snow to study the preservation of meat — an early experimental death.

events.title: Parthenon Completed
events.blurb: A marble temple dedicated to the patron goddess of an Athenian acropolis was completed after fifteen years of work. The structure refined classical Doric proportions, incorporated subtle optical corrections (all its columns lean slightly inward, curved "entasis" swelling their shafts) so the temple appears perfectly rectilinear from a distance, and housed a 12-metre ivory-and-gold statue of Athena. It stood substantially intact for over 2,000 years until a Venetian shell hit a Turkish powder magazine inside it in 1687.
events.revealBlurb: 438 BCE — Ictinus and Callicrates, architects, under Phidias as sculptor. Built on the acropolis of Athens under Pericles. The Elgin Marbles, sold to the British Museum in 1816, are fragments of the Parthenon's sculptural programme — still the subject of Greek repatriation demands.

events.title: Pont du Gard Built
events.blurb: A three-tiered limestone aqueduct bridge was constructed to carry water 50 kilometres across southern Gaul to the Roman colony of Nemausus (modern Nîmes). The top level — 48 metres above the River Gard — still carried its channel; the whole structure spans 275 metres. It was built dry, without mortar, using stones so precisely cut that the joints remain watertight after two millennia. The aqueduct itself was decommissioned in the 6th century; the bridge survived as a road crossing.
events.revealBlurb: c. 50 CE — built under Emperor Claudius. The water it carried had a gradient of only 1 in 3,000 — about 30 centimetres of drop per kilometre. The Pont du Gard is now a UNESCO World Heritage Site and one of the most visited tourist destinations in France.

events.title: Forbidden City Completed
events.blurb: A Ming-dynasty emperor completed an imperial palace complex at the center of his new northern capital — 980 buildings, 9,999 rooms, on a site of 72 hectares, enclosed by a moat and a 10-metre wall. It served as the home and ceremonial centre of 24 successive emperors across two dynasties. The compound was closed to the public for 500 years; it was opened as a museum after the abdication of the last Qing emperor in 1912.
events.revealBlurb: 1420 — the Yongle Emperor, completing the move of the Ming capital from Nanjing to Beijing. Over a million workers built it in 14 years. The last emperor to live there was Puyi, who was expelled in 1924. It is now China's most-visited museum.

events.title: Chrysler Building Completed
events.blurb: A 319-metre Manhattan skyscraper, topped with a radiator-cap-inspired sunburst spire, opened at the corner of 42nd Street and Lexington Avenue as the tallest building in the world. Its automotive-magnate patron had kept the spire a construction secret; it was assembled inside the tower's upper levels and then hoisted into place in 90 minutes, triumphing over a rival bank project down Wall Street that had briefly claimed the height title. The Empire State Building eclipsed it 11 months later.
events.revealBlurb: May 27, 1930 — architect William Van Alen for Walter Chrysler. The Art Deco ornamentation includes eagle gargoyles at the 61st floor and a 1,700-square-metre ceiling mural in the lobby. Van Alen was never paid his fee — Chrysler accused him of taking bribes from suppliers.

events.title: Sydney Opera House Opens
events.blurb: A sail-shaped performing-arts complex on a harbour peninsula opened after 14 years of construction — ten times its original budget and nine years late. The Danish architect had won the design competition in 1957 but resigned in 1966 after political attacks and budget fights; he never saw the completed building. Its concrete "sails," covered in a million tiles of two shades of white, immediately made it one of the most recognized buildings in the world.
events.revealBlurb: October 20, 1973 — architect Jørn Utzon; opened by Queen Elizabeth II. Utzon was eventually reconciled with the building in 1999, 25 years after he left; he was awarded the Pritzker Prize in 2003 but never saw the interior of his own building. It is now a UNESCO World Heritage Site.

events.title: First Public Film Screening
events.blurb: Two French brothers, sons of a portrait photographer, held the first commercial screening of projected motion pictures in the basement of a Paris café. The audience of 33 paid one franc each to watch ten short films — workers leaving a factory, a baby being fed, a boat leaving a harbor. Their cinematograph was both camera and projector; the film was 35mm. Within a year their operators were touring every continent.
events.revealBlurb: December 28, 1895 — Louis and Auguste Lumière at the Salon Indien du Grand Café, Paris. The apocryphal story that audiences ran screaming from the train-arriving film comes from a later screening. The Lumières thought cinema was "an invention without a future" and quickly moved on to other projects.

events.title: Tokyo Story Released
events.blurb: A Japanese director released a 136-minute film about an elderly provincial couple who travel to the capital to visit their adult children, only to find them too busy with their own lives. Its stationary low-angle camera, dialogues shot face-on toward the audience, and refusal of conventional emotional climax embodied the director's signature style. Polls of international critics and filmmakers regularly rank it among the greatest films ever made.
events.revealBlurb: November 3, 1953 — Yasujirō Ozu. He developed the "tatami-level" camera position — 30 cm off the ground, corresponding to the height of a person seated on a tatami mat. It did not gain a Western reputation until the 1970s; Ozu had died in 1963, never having lived to see his international recognition.

events.title: Breathless Released
events.blurb: A 29-year-old French film critic turned director released a 90-minute crime film about a petty thief on the run in Paris with his American girlfriend, shot on handheld camera using natural light, jump cuts, and improvised dialogue. The film's insouciant rulebreaking embodied a new generation of European filmmaking, christened the "Nouvelle Vague" by a critic five years earlier. It made its star into the archetype of post-war cool.
events.revealBlurb: March 16, 1960 — Jean-Luc Godard, starring Jean-Paul Belmondo and Jean Seberg. The famously jarring jump-cuts emerged from an editing crisis: the film was too long and Godard simply removed shots rather than shorten scenes.

events.title: Pulp Fiction Released
events.blurb: A 31-year-old American director released a 154-minute crime picture with a deliberately non-linear structure, three loosely interwoven storylines, and dialogue about hamburgers, foot massages, and divine intervention. It had cost $8 million, been passed on by multiple studios, and been rescued by a new boutique distributor. It won the top prize at Cannes, grossed over $200 million, and pulled a whole generation of independent filmmakers into its wake.
events.revealBlurb: October 14, 1994 — Quentin Tarantino, released by Miramax. The opening Cannes screening received a 15-minute standing ovation. John Travolta's comeback, the soundtrack's surf-rock revival, and the dance scene became instant cultural touchstones.

events.title: Toy Story Released
events.blurb: A California animation studio released the first feature film produced entirely with computer-generated imagery, a 81-minute buddy comedy about a child's cowboy doll who feels threatened by a new space-ranger action figure. The studio had spent four years on the film, through three near-cancellations and total rewrites; the resulting picture grossed $390 million and established a new production studio as the dominant force in animation for the next two decades.
events.revealBlurb: November 22, 1995 — Pixar Animation Studios, directed by John Lasseter. Tom Hanks and Tim Allen voiced Woody and Buzz Lightyear. Pixar had been Apple founder Steve Jobs's expensive side-project; Disney bought them for $7.4 billion in 2006.

events.title: Battle of Salamis
events.blurb: A Greek allied fleet of roughly 370 triremes, lured into position by a false message from the Athenian commander, engaged a Persian fleet of perhaps 800 in the narrow straits between a small island and the Athenian mainland coast. The Persian ships, crowded in the strait, could not maneuver; the Greek triremes rammed them methodically for twelve hours. Over 200 Persian ships were sunk or captured. The Persian king watched the disaster unfold from a throne on the adjacent mainland.
events.revealBlurb: September 480 BCE — Themistocles, Athenian strategos. The Persian king was Xerxes I; he retreated to Asia with much of his army, leaving a smaller force that was destroyed at Plataea the following year. Aeschylus, who had fought at Salamis himself, wrote a play about it eight years later.

events.title: Peloponnesian War Begins
events.blurb: Tensions between a democratic maritime empire led by Athens and an aristocratic land-based league led by Sparta erupted into open war when Spartan forces invaded Athenian-allied territory. The war would last 27 years, consume Greek wealth, shatter Athenian power, and undermine Greek confidence in the democratic project. A historian who had commanded an Athenian force early in the war produced a narrative account considered a founding masterpiece of Western historiography.
events.revealBlurb: 431 BCE — Athens vs. Sparta. The historian was Thucydides. A plague in 430 BCE killed perhaps a quarter of the Athenian population, including the city's leader Pericles. Athens finally surrendered in 404 BCE after its fleet was destroyed at Aegospotami; Socrates was executed in Athens five years later.

events.title: Hannibal Crosses the Alps
events.blurb: A 29-year-old Carthaginian general marched an army of 50,000 men, 9,000 cavalry, and 37 war elephants from Iberia over the Alps into northern Italy over 15 days of early winter, intending to take the war to Rome's home territory. Half his men died in the crossing from cold, hunger, and hostile Alpine tribes. The force that did make it to Italy shocked Rome by winning three successive battles within two years, annihilating Roman legions at Trebbia, Lake Trasimene, and Cannae.
events.revealBlurb: 218 BCE — Hannibal Barca. The exact Alpine pass he used is still debated; the leading candidates are the Col de la Traversette or the Col du Mont Cenis. Only a few elephants made it across and most died in Italy's wet winter. Hannibal won tactically but could not take Rome itself.

events.title: Silk Road Opens
events.blurb: A Chinese imperial envoy returning from a long mission into Central Asia reported the existence of advanced civilizations to the west. His court began dispatching trade missions through the oasis routes of Central Asia; within a century, Chinese silk was appearing in Roman markets, and Mediterranean glass was showing up in Han-dynasty tombs. The overland trade network — not a single road but a braided complex — would carry goods, people, religions, and epidemics across Eurasia for 1,500 years.
events.revealBlurb: c. 130 BCE — Zhang Qian's second mission, under Emperor Wu of Han. The term "Silk Road" was coined by 19th-century German geographer Ferdinand von Richthofen; no one in antiquity used the phrase. Buddhism reached China along it; the Black Death would as well.

events.title: Julius Caesar Assassinated
events.blurb: A Roman dictator, having been named dictator-for-life a month earlier, was stabbed 23 times by a group of 60 senators at a meeting of the Senate held in a Pompey-built theatre. The assassins, styling themselves "Liberators," had convinced themselves that removing the man who had effectively ended the Republic would restore it. Instead, his death plunged Rome into 14 more years of civil war, at the end of which his adopted heir emerged as the first Roman emperor in all but name.
events.revealBlurb: March 15, 44 BCE — the Ides of March. Conspirators included Brutus and Cassius. The supposed last words "Et tu, Brute?" come from Shakespeare; Caesar's actual last words — if he spoke any — may have been the Greek "kai su, teknon?" ("you too, my child?"). His heir Octavian defeated the conspirators at Philippi two years later.

events.title: Windows 1.0 Released
events.blurb: An American software company released a graphical shell running on top of its text-based operating system, intended to compete with the Macintosh's point-and-click interface on IBM PC-compatible machines. Reviewers found the product clunky and slow; the original windows could not overlap, only tile side by side. Most of the PC industry continued using DOS alone for several years. Six years and three major revisions later, version 3.0 finally broke through.
events.revealBlurb: November 20, 1985 — Microsoft Windows 1.0. Product manager Tandy Trower had to beg Gates to ship it; internally there had been talk of cancelling the project. Apple sued Microsoft in 1988 over interface similarities; Apple eventually lost after six years.

events.title: iMac Released
events.blurb: A California computer company, newly returned to profitability under a recently returned co-founder, released an all-in-one desktop machine housed in a translucent Bondi-blue plastic case, with no floppy drive, a built-in USB port, and a round puck of a mouse. Industrial designer Jonathan Ive had led the design. The machine was derided on spec by some industry press; it sold over 800,000 units in the first five months and rescued the company's consumer business.
events.revealBlurb: August 15, 1998 — Apple iMac G3, designed by Jonathan Ive under Steve Jobs. The "i" prefix, coined by copywriter Ken Segall, would carry over to iPod, iPhone, iPad, iCloud. The translucent plastic shell was revolutionary for its time.

events.title: iPod Launched
events.blurb: A California computer company released a white portable music player with a 5 GB hard drive — "1,000 songs in your pocket," according to its co-founder's introduction — and a scrollwheel for navigation. The industry press was unimpressed; smaller MP3 players already existed. Over the next decade, the iPod and its derivatives would sell over 400 million units, reshape the music industry, and serve as a forerunner and technological foundation for the iPhone.
events.revealBlurb: October 23, 2001 — Apple iPod. Steve Jobs introduced it at a small press event, not to a large keynote crowd. Initial reviews focused on how it was Mac-only; the 2003 Windows version opened the floodgates.

events.title: iPhone Announced
events.blurb: A California computer company's co-founder unveiled a new class of mobile phone at a San Francisco conference, combining a widescreen iPod, a mobile internet browser, and a phone into a single slim device controlled entirely by a multi-touch finger-driven screen. He dialled a coffee shop on stage to demonstrate. Nokia's executives watching the announcement reportedly laughed at its lack of a physical keyboard; BlackBerry's CEO later admitted they also underestimated it.
events.revealBlurb: January 9, 2007 — Steve Jobs at Macworld. It went on sale June 29. The original did not support 3G, had no copy-and-paste, and shipped without an App Store — those all came in subsequent years. Apple now makes over $200 billion a year just from iPhones.

events.title: First Android Phone Released
events.blurb: A Taiwanese handset maker released the first commercial phone running an open-source mobile operating system developed by a Silicon Valley search-engine company, available through a US mobile carrier. The device had a physical keyboard that slid out from under the screen; unlike the rival iPhone, users could install apps from anywhere, replace the default apps, and generally modify the device at will. Open-ecosystem Android would grow to dominate global smartphone market share.
events.revealBlurb: October 22, 2008 — T-Mobile G1 (HTC Dream), running Android 1.0. Google had quietly acquired Android Inc. for $50 million in 2005. By 2013 more than half of smartphones sold ran Android; today it's over 70 percent globally.

events.title: Boston Tea Party
events.blurb: That winter night, some 116 colonists disguised as Mohawk warriors boarded three ships in Boston Harbor and dumped 342 chests of East India Company tea into the water, destroying approximately £10,000 worth of merchandise. The targeted destruction was a direct protest against the Tea Act, which granted the company a monopoly while taxing colonial consumers.
events.revealBlurb: December 16, 1773 — Boston Harbor. Not a single participant was ever prosecuted. Britain's furious response — the Coercive Acts, which colonists renamed the Intolerable Acts — did more to unify colonial resistance than the tea party itself. The name "Boston Tea Party" wasn't coined until decades later.

events.title: British Surrender at Saratoga
events.blurb: A British army of 6,000 men under a genteel general who had marched south from Canada intending to split the American colonies along the Hudson Valley found itself encircled at a rural New York hamlet after two pitched battles and dwindling supplies. The general surrendered his entire force to the American commander. It was the most consequential Allied success of the war; France, which had been secretly aiding the colonies, publicly entered the conflict four months later.
events.revealBlurb: October 17, 1777 — British general John Burgoyne surrenders to American general Horatio Gates. Burgoyne had been marching from Canada; a complementary British push up the Hudson from New York had been misdirected to Pennsylvania. The victory secured French diplomatic recognition and military alliance.

events.title: Cornwallis Surrenders at Yorktown
events.blurb: A British army of 8,000 men under a peer of the realm, trapped on a Virginia peninsula by a combined Franco-American land force and blocked from the Chesapeake by a French fleet, surrendered after a three-week siege. The British commander, reportedly feigning illness, sent a deputy to the surrender ceremony; his band played a tune called "The World Turned Upside Down." The war dragged on in minor engagements for two more years but the outcome was no longer in doubt.
events.revealBlurb: October 19, 1781 — Lord Cornwallis surrenders to General George Washington and Comte de Rochambeau at Yorktown, Virginia. The French navy's blockade, commanded by Admiral de Grasse, decided the siege. Formal peace negotiations began within months.

events.title: Haitian Revolution Begins
events.blurb: A voodoo ceremony in a wooded area of a French Caribbean sugar colony marked the coordinated signal for a mass uprising of enslaved Africans. Within ten days, plantations across the northern plain were in flames and 4,000 whites and mulattos were dead. It was the largest slave revolt in the history of the Americas and the only one that successfully established an independent state. The colony had been the richest in the Western hemisphere; it produced 40 percent of the world's sugar.
events.revealBlurb: August 22, 1791 — Saint-Domingue (now Haiti). The ceremony was at Bois Caïman, led by voodoo priest Dutty Boukman. Toussaint Louverture emerged as principal leader, though he was captured by the French in 1802 and died in a freezing French prison cell. Independence came on January 1, 1804.

events.title: Napoleon Crowned Emperor
events.blurb: A 35-year-old Corsican-born general, having ruled France as First Consul for five years, staged a coronation at the Gothic cathedral in the French capital. He had negotiated the pope's attendance; in the ceremony's most famous moment — possibly prearranged, possibly improvised — the emperor took the crown from the pope and placed it on his own head. The act was read as a message: no religious authority ratified his power.
events.revealBlurb: December 2, 1804 — Notre-Dame de Paris. Pope Pius VII had been brought from Rome; he sat largely passive through the ceremony. Napoleon's wife Joséphine also crowned herself empress. Jacques-Louis David's monumental painting of the coronation, finished three years later, flatters Napoleon's height among other details.

events.title: Alien and Sedition Acts Signed
events.blurb: President John Adams signed four statutes that extended the residency requirement for citizenship from five to fourteen years, empowered the president to expel foreigners deemed dangerous, and made it a crime to publish "false, scandalous, and malicious" criticism of the government. The laws were aimed largely at French immigrants and Republican newspaper editors who opposed the Federalist administration.
events.revealBlurb: July 14, 1798 — Philadelphia (the Sedition Act, last of the four). Twenty-five people were arrested and ten convicted under the Sedition Act — all of them Jefferson's supporters. Jefferson himself quietly wrote the Kentucky Resolutions arguing states could nullify federal law.

events.title: Marbury v. Madison: Judicial Review Established
events.blurb: Chief Justice John Marshall wrote the unanimous Supreme Court opinion in a case about a disputed judicial appointment, using it to announce that federal courts possessed the power to strike down laws they found incompatible with the Constitution — a power the Constitution itself does not explicitly mention. The ruling transformed the Supreme Court from the weakest branch of government into an equal arbiter of constitutional meaning.
events.revealBlurb: February 24, 1803 — Washington, D.C. Marshall's genius was ruling against Marbury (who wanted his commission) so Jefferson couldn't refuse to comply, while simultaneously claiming the Court's enormous new power. Jefferson privately hated the decision but was trapped. The ruling wasn't used to strike down another law for 54 more years.

events.title: Missouri Compromise Signed
events.blurb: President James Monroe signed legislation admitting Missouri as a slave state and Maine as a free state simultaneously, preserving the Senate balance between slave and free states, and drawing an invisible line across the continent at latitude 36°30' north — prohibiting slavery in all remaining territory of the Louisiana Purchase above that line.
events.revealBlurb: March 6, 1820 — Washington, D.C. Thomas Jefferson, then 76, called the Missouri debate "a fire bell in the night" that terrified him. The 36°30' line held for 34 years before the Kansas-Nebraska Act erased it in 1854.

events.title: Wall Street Crash: Black Tuesday
events.blurb: On the 29th of that month, stock markets collapsed in a cascade of panic selling that wiped out an estimated $14 billion in a single day, erasing the paper fortunes of thousands of investors and devastating the banking system. The crash followed years of rampant speculation fueled by easy credit and margin buying, in which millions of Americans had purchased stocks with borrowed money against collateral that suddenly no longer existed.
events.revealBlurb: October 29, 1929 — New York Stock Exchange. More than 16 million shares traded on Black Tuesday — a record that stood for decades. The Dow lost nearly 50% of its value by mid-November. Economists still debate whether the crash caused the Great Depression or merely triggered an underlying structural collapse.

events.title: Cuban Missile Crisis: JFK Announces Naval Blockade
events.blurb: On the 22nd of that month, President John F. Kennedy delivered a nationally televised address revealing that U.S. reconnaissance aircraft had discovered Soviet nuclear missile installations under construction in Cuba — 90 miles from Florida — and announcing a naval "quarantine" to prevent further weapons deliveries. For 13 days, the United States and Soviet Union stood closer to nuclear war than at any other moment in history before or since.
events.revealBlurb: October 22, 1962 — Washington, D.C. Kennedy called it a "quarantine" because a blockade is an act of war under international law. Soviet ships turned around on October 24. The secret resolution involved the U.S. quietly removing its Jupiter missiles from Turkey — a concession Kennedy couldn't publicly acknowledge for decades.

events.title: Battle of Zama
events.blurb: Scipio Africanus neutralised Hannibal's 80 war elephants by opening lanes in his formation so they stampeded harmlessly through, then used superior cavalry to encircle the Carthaginian infantry. Roughly 20,000 Carthaginians died; Carthage accepted a peace stripping it of its fleet, all war elephants, and 10,000 silver talents paid over fifty years.
events.revealBlurb: October 19, 202 BCE, North Africa. This was the only time in Hannibal's career that his battle plan failed. After the war, Scipio received the cognomen "Africanus"; his grateful soldiers offered to make him king of Rome, which he refused.

events.title: Aurelian Reunifies the Empire
events.blurb: After the empire had fractured into three competing states, Emperor Aurelian defeated the Palmyrene Empire in the east — capturing its queen Zenobia — and then the breakaway Gallic Empire in the west, bringing Britain, Gaul, Spain, Syria, and Egypt back under a single ruler within five years of taking power. He then began building a massive new defensive wall around Rome itself.
events.revealBlurb: 274 CE. Queen Zenobia of Palmyra had claimed descent from Cleopatra and ruled a sophisticated court of scholars and poets while commanding legions across the Near East. After capture she was eventually settled near Tivoli and, according to some sources, married a Roman senator.

events.title: Theodosius Makes Christianity the Sole Legal Religion
events.blurb: Emperor Theodosius issued a series of decrees that outlawed public pagan sacrifice, closed all temples, extinguished the sacred fire of Vesta, disbanded the Vestal Virgins, and ended the Olympic Games. Christianity, which had been a persecuted sect three generations earlier, was now the only lawful religion of the Roman Empire.
events.revealBlurb: 391 CE. The Olympic Games, which had run continuously for over a thousand years, ended because Theodosius considered them a pagan festival — they were not revived until 1896. The fire of Vesta had burned in the Forum for centuries; snuffing it out was treated as a rupture with Rome's foundational identity.

events.title: Attila Invades Italy
events.blurb: Hunnic forces under Attila crossed the Alps, razed the wealthy port city of Aquileia so completely it was never rebuilt, and sacked Milan and Pavia before advancing toward Rome itself. Pope Leo I led a diplomatic mission to meet Attila on the banks of the Mincio River; Attila withdrew without attacking Rome, though historians debate whether Leo, disease, famine, or approaching eastern armies deserved the credit.
events.revealBlurb: Summer 452 CE. Aquileia had been one of the richest cities in the western empire; legend says its refugees founded Venice on the lagoon islands to escape the Huns. Attila died the following year on his wedding night — of a nosebleed, according to ancient sources.

events.title: Deposition of Romulus Augustulus
events.blurb: The Germanic warlord Odoacer deposed the sixteen-year-old emperor Romulus Augustulus at Ravenna — a boy whose mocking nickname meant "Little Augustus" — and sent the imperial regalia to Constantinople, informing the eastern emperor that the west no longer needed a separate ruler. Odoacer spared Romulus's life, finding him too young and too minor to bother executing, and exiled him to a villa in Campania on a pension.
events.revealBlurb: September 4, 476 CE. The last western emperor's name combined the city's legendary founder and its first emperor — an irony Roman writers noticed immediately. Contemporaries did not regard this moment as "the fall of Rome"; that framing came centuries later. The eastern empire in Constantinople continued for another 977 years.

events.title: Angkor Wat Completed
events.blurb: A Khmer king completed a vast temple complex in his capital, originally dedicated to the Hindu god Vishnu and later converted to Buddhist use. Covering over 160 hectares, surrounded by a moat, topped with a central tower 65 metres high, and decorated with 1.6 kilometres of bas-relief carvings illustrating Hindu epics, it was the largest religious monument in the world. After the Khmer capital shifted in the 15th century, the jungle gradually overgrew the complex, which was rediscovered by European travellers in the 19th century.
events.revealBlurb: c. 1150 — King Suryavarman II, in the capital of the Khmer Empire (modern Cambodia). It appears on the Cambodian flag — the only national flag featuring a building. French explorer Henri Mouhot's 1861 account brought it to Western attention, though it had never actually been "lost."

events.title: Taj Mahal Completed
events.blurb: A Mughal emperor completed, 22 years after his beloved queen's death in childbirth, a white-marble mausoleum for her on the bank of a river in a North Indian city. Some 20,000 craftsmen worked on the main structure alone; the dome rises 73 metres, inlaid with semiprecious stones in floral and calligraphic patterns. A matching mosque flanks one side of the tomb; a guest house mirrors it on the other. The emperor's own body joined hers in the crypt in 1666.
events.revealBlurb: c. 1648 — Shah Jahan for Mumtaz Mahal, who died in 1631. The architectural team was led by Ustad Ahmad Lahori. An apocryphal legend claims Shah Jahan cut off the master builders' hands; there is no historical evidence for it. The monument changes colour subtly throughout the day.

events.title: St. Paul's Cathedral Completed
events.blurb: After 35 years of construction replacing a medieval cathedral destroyed in the Great Fire of London, a 68-year-old English architect watched his son install the final piece of his new cathedral's lantern atop its dome — the first cathedral anywhere in the world to have been entirely designed, built, and completed by a single architect within his own lifetime. The triple-domed design, inspired by St. Peter's in Rome, rose 111 metres above the City of London.
events.revealBlurb: 1710 — Sir Christopher Wren. He also designed 52 other London churches after the Great Fire of 1666. He was buried in the cathedral's crypt when he died in 1723 at 90; his memorial reads "Si monumentum requiris, circumspice" — if you seek his monument, look around you.

events.title: Sagrada Família Begun
events.blurb: Construction began on a Catholic basilica in the Catalan capital, funded by donations alone — a condition that would stretch the project across a century and a half. The original architect was replaced after one year by a 31-year-old ferociously religious designer who would pour the rest of his life into the project, combining Gothic and Art Nouveau influences into a style of his own. He would die 43 years later, hit by a tram on the street outside; only a fraction of the church was finished. Construction continues today.
events.revealBlurb: March 19, 1882 — original architect Francisco de Paula del Villar; succeeded 1883 by Antoni Gaudí. Gaudí devoted the last 15 years of his life exclusively to the project. He was hit by a tram on June 7, 1926; his grave is in the crypt. Completion is projected for 2026 — a century after his death.

events.title: Fallingwater Completed
events.blurb: A 70-year-old American architect completed a weekend house for a Pittsburgh department-store owner, cantilevered dramatically over a waterfall in rural western Pennsylvania. The design — with horizontal reinforced-concrete terraces seemingly floating over the rock and water — reimagined what residential architecture could be and became a singular icon of 20th-century organic architecture. The cantilevered decks began sagging within years; an expensive 21st-century restoration saved the house.
events.revealBlurb: 1937 — Frank Lloyd Wright for the Kaufmann family in Bear Run, PA. The Kaufmanns had expected the house to sit across from the waterfall looking at it; Wright insisted on placing it over the water. Wright won the Gold Medal of the Royal Institute of British Architects in 1941 and the AIA Gold Medal in 1949.

events.title: First Transatlantic Telegraph Cable
events.blurb: After two previous attempts failed mid-Atlantic, a joint American-British consortium successfully laid a 3,700-kilometre copper cable across the ocean floor between Ireland and Newfoundland. The Queen of England and the President of the United States exchanged the first messages. The cable's signal degraded rapidly — the 99-word inaugural message took 17 hours to send — and the cable failed entirely within three weeks, but the feasibility had been proved.
events.revealBlurb: August 5, 1858 — the cable was completed; August 16, the first messages between Queen Victoria and President James Buchanan. The project's main backer, American financier Cyrus West Field, persisted through four failed attempts and finally established a durable cable in 1866. His Atlantic cables cut communication between continents from weeks to minutes.

events.title: US Transcontinental Railroad Completed
events.blurb: Officials drove a ceremonial golden spike into a rail tie at a desolate spot in Utah, joining rails built eastward from Sacramento by Chinese labourers and rails built westward from the Missouri River by Irish labourers. Travel from New York to San Francisco, previously a six-month journey by wagon or ship, now took a week. The two companies, a state-subsidized joint venture, had raced each other for six years; the route had been set by the Lincoln administration in 1862.
events.revealBlurb: May 10, 1869 — Promontory Summit, Utah. The joining rails were two: Central Pacific from the west, Union Pacific from the east. The spike ceremony was telegraphed to the rest of the country; the "Done" message was the first cross-country news bulletin. The Chinese workers who had done most of the hardest labour were not invited to the ceremony.

events.title: Edison's Practical Lightbulb
events.blurb: After 14 months of systematic experimentation with thousands of possible filament materials — and many previous lightbulb designs by other inventors — an American inventor's laboratory team achieved a 40-hour burn using a carbonized cotton-thread filament in an evacuated glass bulb. The achievement's significance was not inventing the lightbulb itself (which had existed in various forms for decades) but making one that burned long enough to be commercially viable.
events.revealBlurb: October 21, 1879 — Thomas Edison at Menlo Park. His 1880 improved version used a bamboo filament and burned 1,200 hours. Edison's real genius was less invention than the systematic industrial R&D lab he created — the template for every modern corporate research operation.

events.title: Benz Patents the Motorwagen
events.blurb: A 41-year-old German mechanical engineer filed a patent for a three-wheeled vehicle powered by a single-cylinder internal combustion engine of his own design. The machine, producing about 2/3 of a horsepower, could reach a top speed of 16 km/h. His wife Bertha took it on an unauthorized 106-kilometre cross-country trip two years later without telling him, demonstrating its practicality; the publicity helped launch the commercial automobile industry.
events.revealBlurb: January 29, 1886 — Karl Benz, Mannheim.
