Bertha's 1888 trip required her to refuel at apothecaries (selling ligroin, a cleaning solvent, as the only available fuel) and improvise brake repairs using her garter as an insulator. Benz's company later merged with Daimler's to form Mercedes-Benz.

events.title: Eiffel Tower Opens
events.blurb: A 300-metre wrought-iron lattice tower, built over two years, two months, and five days as the entrance arch to a Paris world's fair, was completed. At three times the height of the Washington Monument, it was the tallest man-made structure in the world and would remain so for 41 years. A petition signed by 300 prominent French artists had protested the "useless and monstrous" project during construction. It was intended to be demolished after 20 years; radio antennas saved it.
events.revealBlurb: March 31, 1889 — designed by Gustave Eiffel for the 1889 Exposition Universelle, marking the centennial of the French Revolution. It remained the tallest building until the 1930 Chrysler Building. The Nazi occupation cut the elevator cables; Parisians said the "Hitler had to climb the stairs to the top."

events.title: Trinity Nuclear Test
events.blurb: A plutonium implosion device was detonated atop a 30-metre steel tower in the New Mexico desert, producing a fireball visible 160 kilometres away and an explosion equivalent to 21 kilotons of TNT. Watching from a bunker 16 kilometres distant, the project's scientific director later recalled a verse from Hindu scripture about becoming death, destroyer of worlds.

events.title: Hungarian Revolution
events.blurb: A student demonstration in Budapest grew within hours into a nationwide uprising against a Moscow-backed government. For twelve days, a reform-minded premier announced democratic elections and withdrawal from the eastern bloc military alliance. Then 2,500 Soviet tanks rolled into the country, crushing the revolt and killing some 2,500 Hungarians.
events.revealBlurb: October 23 to November 10, 1956 — reform premier Imre Nagy was tricked into a "negotiation," arrested, and secretly executed two years later. 200,000 Hungarians fled west. The West's failure to intervene exposed the limits of containment.

events.title: Cuban Missile Crisis Address
events.blurb: An American president delivered a 17-minute televised address revealing that Soviet nuclear missiles had been discovered on a Caribbean island 145 kilometres from Florida, demanding their removal within a strict deadline. The 13-day standoff that followed was the closest the Cold War came to nuclear exchange, with submarines on both sides carrying armed torpedoes.

events.title: SALT I Signed
events.blurb: In the ornate Vladimir Hall of the Kremlin, the leaders of the two superpowers signed the first treaty limiting strategic nuclear weapons. It froze the number of intercontinental and submarine-launched ballistic missiles on each side at then-current levels and restricted anti-missile defenses. Neither arsenal shrank, but the race for ever more warheads finally acquired guardrails.
events.revealBlurb: May 26, 1972 — Nixon and Brezhnev in Moscow. The ABM Treaty signed the same day restricted each side to two (later one) missile defense sites. The US withdrew from it in 2002 under George W. Bush.

events.title: Helsinki Accords
events.blurb: Thirty-five nations — every European country except tiny Albania, plus the U.S. and Canada — signed a sweeping final act in the Finnish capital that acknowledged post-war borders while binding signatories to respect human rights. Critics called it a sellout to Moscow. In fact, its human rights provisions gave eastern dissidents a legal framework that would undermine the regimes a decade later.
events.revealBlurb: August 1, 1975 — the "Third Basket" on human rights proved subversive. Czech dissidents founded Charter 77 using its language; the Moscow Helsinki Group followed. Brezhnev didn't realize he'd just signed his system's eventual death warrant.

events.title: V-2 Rocket's First Successful Test
events.blurb: A 14-metre liquid-fuelled rocket rose from a Baltic coast test site, climbed above the atmosphere, and travelled 190 kilometres before splashing down — the first object built by human hands to reach space, demonstrating a weapon that could strike cities at supersonic speed with no interception possible by any existing technology.
events.revealBlurb: October 3, 1942, Peenemünde. General Walter Dornberger declared: "This third day of October is the first day of a new era, that of space travel." The same technology later launched the first satellites and moon rockets. The V-2's wartime manufacture killed more people in slave-labour production than it killed as a weapon.

events.title: Second Battle of El Alamein
events.blurb: A British commander who had spent three months rebuilding his army launched a night artillery barrage from 1,000 guns and began grinding through minefields and fortified positions across the Egyptian desert, slowly destroying an Axis force that had driven to within 100 kilometres of a strategically critical port city.
events.revealBlurb: October 23 – November 4, 1942. Montgomery's artillery fired 529,000 shells in the opening barrage. Rommel was on sick leave in Austria when the battle opened; Hitler ordered him back by telegram. After twelve days, Rommel began a 2,000-kilometre retreat across North Africa that ended with final Axis surrender in Tunisia six months later.

events.title: Battle of Leyte Gulf
events.blurb: Over four days, 282 warships clashed in four separate engagements across several hundred thousand square kilometres of open ocean — the largest naval battle in history by tonnage and personnel — as one navy committed virtually everything it had left to stop an invasion and the other deployed over 300 ships to press it through.
events.revealBlurb: October 23–26, 1944. Japan used its remaining fleet carriers as decoys with almost no aircraft aboard. A small force of US destroyers and escort carriers somehow bluffed a vastly superior Japanese battleship force into retreating at the Battle of Samar — one of the most improbable tactical reversals of the war. Japan also deployed kamikaze suicide aircraft in force for the first time.

events.title: Potsdam Conference
events.blurb: The three great powers met for the last time in an occupied defeated nation's suburbs, dividing it into occupation zones, setting reparations terms, and issuing an ultimatum to a remaining Asian adversary — while one leader discreetly mentioned to another that his country had recently successfully tested a weapon of extraordinary destructive power, which the other already knew about from spies.
events.revealBlurb: July 17 – August 2, 1945. Truman told Stalin the US had "a new weapon of unusual destructive force" — Trinity had been tested the previous day. Stalin showed no reaction; his spies had briefed him months earlier. Churchill lost the British general election mid-conference and was replaced by Clement Attlee, who turned up having learned the secrets only days before.

events.title: Atomic Bombing of Hiroshima
events.blurb: A single aircraft flying at high altitude released a single bomb over a mid-sized city at 8:15 in the morning, detonating it 600 metres above a distinctive T-shaped bridge with the force of 15,000 tons of TNT — flattening 13 square kilometres, killing between 70,000 and 80,000 people instantly, and ultimately causing 140,000 deaths by the end of the year.
events.revealBlurb: August 6, 1945 — B-29 Enola Gay, piloted by Colonel Paul Tibbets, dropped "Little Boy" over Hiroshima. The aiming point was the Aioi Bridge. The bomb missed by about 250 metres but it did not matter. Tibbets's mother's name was Enola Gay. The co-pilot, Robert Lewis, wrote in his journal: "My God, what have we done?"

events.title: Nintendo Famicom Launches in Japan
events.blurb: A cheap red-and-white 8-bit console hit Japanese shelves the same day as a competing machine. Within a year it had outsold every rival combined, driven fourteen manufacturers out of the market entirely, and established Nintendo as the unchallenged ruler of the Japanese gaming business.
events.revealBlurb: July 15, 1983 — Nintendo's Family Computer launched in Japan at ¥14,800, head-to-head with Sega's SG-1000. The NES version launched in New York in October 1985. The NES/Famicom line sold 61.91 million units worldwide.

events.title: Nintendo Game Boy Launches in North America
events.blurb: Competing handhelds boasted colour screens and better hardware. Nintendo shipped a grey brick with a pea-green LCD and bundled it with a Soviet puzzle game about falling tetrominoes. The grey brick won. Within weeks every unit in the United States had sold out.
events.revealBlurb: July 31, 1989 — The Game Boy launched in North America at $89.99, selling 40,000 units on day one. The Game Boy line eventually sold 118 million units. The Japan launch had been April 21, 1989.

events.title: Nintendo Virtual Boy Launches
events.blurb: Nintendo shipped a head-mounted gaming console that displayed games in monochrome red on a black background, required users to lean into a stationary visor on a table, and carried a liability warning that it could cause headaches, eye strain, nausea, and seizures. It sold fewer than 800,000 units worldwide before being discontinued.
events.revealBlurb: August 14, 1995 — The Virtual Boy launched in North America at $179.95. Production ceased in December 1995 in Japan — five months after release. Only 22 games were ever published. Gunpei Yokoi left Nintendo the following year and died in a road accident in 1997.

events.title: League of Legends Launches
events.blurb: A free-to-play adaptation of a Warcraft III fan modification launched quietly and grew into the most-played PC game on Earth. At its peak over 100 million accounts had been registered, and its annual World Championship filled football stadiums and drew broadcast audiences that dwarfed traditional sporting events. It invented a new genre name — MOBA — and made esports a career path.
events.revealBlurb: October 27, 2009 — Riot Games released League of Legends in North America. It was free-to-play from day one, monetised through cosmetic skins. The 2019 World Championship Finals drew over 100 million unique viewers. Riot was acquired by Tencent in 2011.

events.title: Red Dead Redemption 2 Released
events.blurb: A cowboy open-world game with a 60-hour main story, simulated beard growth, morality consequences for every interaction, and a horse whose bond with the player affected its responsiveness opened the largest weekend in entertainment history. It earned $725 million in three days.
events.revealBlurb: October 26, 2018 — Red Dead Redemption 2 launched for PlayStation 4 and Xbox One. It shipped 17 million copies in its first thirteen days. The game has now sold over 79 million copies. Development reportedly involved teams working 100-hour weeks across five years.

events.title: Prabhat Film Company Founded
events.blurb: Five filmmakers and one jeweller-financier pooled ₹15,000 in a Kolhapur courtyard and established a studio whose name meant "Dawn" — it would go on to produce landmark Marathi and Hindi films through the 1930s, win the first Venice Film Festival prize awarded to an Asian film, and whose abandoned compound would later house the country's national film school.
events.revealBlurb: June 1, 1929 — founded by V. Shantaram and associates. Their 1936 film Sant Tukaram won a Venice award. When the studio folded in 1953, its Pune premises became the site of the Film and Television Institute of India.

events.title: Kalidas Released — First Tamil Talkie
events.blurb: A mythological musical about the Sanskrit poet Kalidasa opened at Kinema Central in Madras on Diwali and became simultaneously the first sound film in Tamil and the first in Telugu — the hero singing in Telugu, the heroine speaking Tamil, a third actor delivering dialogue in Hindi, making it a multilingual sound experiment disguised as a devotional drama.
events.revealBlurb: October 31, 1931 — directed by H.M. Reddy, just months after Alam Ara introduced sound to India. A young actor billed only as L.V. Prasad played a cameo; he would later become one of South India's most powerful film producers. The film is now preserved at the National Film Archive.

events.title: Mother India Released
events.blurb: A near-three-hour epic about a village woman who spends decades breaking stones, raising sons, and protecting her community from a money-lender opened on Diwali across India and broke every box-office record to that point. The following year it became India's first film nominated for the Academy Award for Best Foreign Language Film — losing by a single vote to a Federico Fellini picture.
events.revealBlurb: October 25, 1957. Directed by Mehboob Khan. Nargis, who plays the mother, married co-star Sunil Dutt after he dragged her unconscious from a fire that broke out on set. Khan's production logo featured a hammer-and-sickle; it was quietly removed before the Oscar submission print.

events.title: Lagaan Nominated for Academy Award
events.blurb: A four-hour cricket epic set under British colonial rule — filmed largely in a Gujarat village with a cast of thousands, shot in Hindi with English-speaking British actors, and assembled into a musical — was selected as India's submission to the Academy Awards and became only the third Indian film in history to receive a Best Foreign Language Film nomination.
events.revealBlurb: Released June 15, 2001; Oscar nomination announced February 2002. Aamir Khan both produced and starred. The film was shot in the searing Bhuj heat over 75 days. Its cricket finale runs 20 minutes and was edited like a sporting thriller — at the time considered unbankably risky for a Bollywood audience.

events.title: Taare Zameen Par Released
events.blurb: A film about an eight-year-old with undiagnosed dyslexia shipped off to boarding school for failing every subject — told largely from the child's hallucinatory perspective — earned ₹98 crore worldwide and prompted school boards across India to introduce dyslexia screening. Its child lead, discovered through an open casting call, had never acted before.
events.revealBlurb: December 21, 2007 — Aamir Khan's directorial debut, having taken over from Amole Gupte mid-production. Darsheel Safary, then 9, auditioned among 1,000 children. The film catalysed new Indian legislation on learning disability accommodation in schools. Khan dedicated the film to every child who had been misunderstood.

events.title: Pac-Man Reaches North America
events.blurb: A Japanese arcade cabinet featuring a yellow circular character navigating a maze while consuming dots and evading four coloured ghosts began distribution across North American arcades. Within 18 months it had been installed in over 100,000 locations and grossed more revenue than all theatrical box office receipts in America that year combined.

events.title: Tylenol Murders
events.blurb: Seven people in the Chicago area died after taking over-the-counter acetaminophen capsules that had been laced with potassium cyanide by an unknown tamperer. The crisis triggered a nationwide recall of 31 million bottles, launched the tamper-resistant packaging industry, and reshaped pharmaceutical manufacturing standards permanently. Johnson & Johnson's swift and transparent response became a classic case study in crisis management. The killer was never identified.
events.revealBlurb: September 29-October 1, 1982 — seven deaths in Chicago suburbs. Pills had been purchased, tampered with, and returned to drugstore shelves. James William Lewis, a former suspect, died in 2023 maintaining his innocence. Tamper-proof packaging became a federal mandate within six months.

events.title: Apple's "1984" Super Bowl Ad
events.blurb: A 60-second commercial produced by a British director for a California computer company aired during the third quarter of the Super Bowl. The ad showed a dystopian audience of grey workers watching a Big-Brother-like speaker on a vast screen; an athletic woman in running clothes smashed the screen with a hammer. The product was the Macintosh computer. Apple's board had voted to kill the ad; the CEO insisted it air. It aired once.
events.revealBlurb: January 22, 1984 — directed by Ridley Scott. The ad ran nationally only that one time; it has since been shown as a promotion or film-clip thousands of times. Macintosh sales in its first 100 days exceeded expectations. The "1984" ad is still considered one of the greatest commercials ever made.

events.title: Challenger Disintegration
events.blurb: Space Shuttle Challenger broke apart 73 seconds after launch when a rubber O-ring seal on the right solid rocket booster failed in overnight temperatures that had dropped to -8 °C, allowing combustion gases to breach the joint and sever the external tank. All seven crew members were killed, including Christa McAuliffe, who had been selected from more than 11,000 applicants for NASA's Teacher in Space program.
events.revealBlurb: January 28, 1986 — STS-51-L. Engineers at Morton Thiokol had urged a launch delay the night before, citing O-ring behavior in cold temperatures; NASA managers overruled them. The crew cabin survived the initial breakup intact and fell for nearly three minutes before striking the Atlantic at roughly 320 km/h.

events.title: Madonna's "Like a Prayer" Video
events.blurb: The music video for a 30-year-old singer's new single, featuring burning crosses, stigmata, and the singer kissing a Black saint statue coming to life, premiered during a Pepsi commercial at the start of a television special paid for by the soft-drink company. The Vatican condemned the video as blasphemous; conservative Christian groups organized boycotts; Pepsi paid the singer $5 million to sever their sponsorship deal. Her album sold 15 million copies.
events.revealBlurb: March 2, 1989 — the Pepsi commercial; the full video premiered on MTV March 3. Director Mary Lambert. The controversy gave Madonna an estimated $5 million for the Pepsi deal plus enormous free publicity; she kept the money. The album "Like a Prayer" remains her best-reviewed.

events.title: First ARPANET Message
events.blurb: A graduate student at a California university tried to log in remotely to a computer at a research institute 560 kilometres north. He typed "L," then "O," then tried to type "G" — and the receiving computer crashed. The first ever message transmitted between two computers on what would grow into the global network was thus the two-letter sequence "lo."
events.revealBlurb: October 29, 1969 — UCLA to the Stanford Research Institute. The student was Charley Kline. ARPANET was funded by the Pentagon to enable communication after a nuclear strike. The network went from 4 nodes to 37 in three years.

events.title: eBay Founded
events.blurb: A 28-year-old Iranian-American software engineer set up an online auction site over the Labor Day weekend, initially as a hobby project on a personal server. One of the first items sold was a broken laser pointer for $14.83. When he emailed the buyer to check whether he understood it was broken, the buyer replied that he collected broken laser pointers. The founder realized he had a business on his hands.
events.revealBlurb: September 3, 1995 — Pierre Omidyar. He originally named it AuctionWeb; renamed eBay in 1997, short for Echo Bay Technology, his consulting firm. The first commission was sent as a personal check for $241.19.

events.title: YouTube Launched
events.blurb: Three former PayPal employees, reportedly frustrated that they couldn't easily share a video of a dinner party or (by an alternate legend) a wardrobe malfunction from a recent sporting event, registered a domain name for a video-sharing site. The site's first uploaded video, "Me at the zoo," was an 18-second clip of one of the founders standing in front of elephants at the San Diego Zoo. Google bought them for $1.65 billion in stock twenty months later.
events.revealBlurb: February 14, 2005 — Chad Hurley, Steve Chen, Jawed Karim. The "Me at the zoo" video is still online, with over 350 million views. Users now upload over 500 hours of video every minute.

events.title: Bitcoin Whitepaper Published
events.blurb: A nine-page academic paper titled "Bitcoin: A Peer-to-Peer Electronic Cash System," written under a pseudonym, was posted to a cryptography mailing list in the middle of the global financial crisis. It described a digital currency that didn't need banks or central authorities to verify transactions. The first block of the currency was mined two months later; the identity of its author has never been established.
events.revealBlurb: October 31, 2008 — "Satoshi Nakamoto." The genesis block, mined January 3, 2009, contained the text "Chancellor on brink of second bailout for banks" from that day's Times. Suspected Satoshis have included Hal Finney, Nick Szabo, Craig Wright (contested), and Dorian Nakamoto (denied).

events.title: Facebook Buys WhatsApp
events.blurb: A Silicon Valley social-networking giant announced an agreement to acquire a five-year-old messaging app with 450 million users for $19 billion in cash and stock — the largest venture-backed acquisition in tech history. The app had 55 employees; one of its two founders had been rejected when he applied for a job at Facebook eight years earlier.
events.revealBlurb: February 19, 2014 — Facebook buys WhatsApp; co-founders Jan Koum and Brian Acton. The service had been run on the principle of no ads, no gimmicks; Acton later left Facebook over disagreements about monetization and funded the rival Signal.

events.title: Pantheon of Rome Completed
events.blurb: A Roman emperor completed a rebuilt temple, topped with an unreinforced concrete dome 43.3 metres in diameter — the largest dome in the world for over 1,300 years, and still the largest unreinforced-concrete dome ever built. A 9-metre oculus at its apex is the only source of natural light. The dome's concrete mix grew lighter toward the top (using pumice aggregate), and its coffered interior thinned as it rose, reducing weight where it mattered.
events.revealBlurb: c. 126 CE — Emperor Hadrian, rebuilding an earlier Agrippa temple destroyed by fire. It became a Catholic church in 609 CE, which is why it survived intact unlike other Roman temples. Raphael and the Italian kings Victor Emmanuel II and Umberto I are buried inside.

events.title: Brunelleschi's Dome Completed
events.blurb: A Florentine goldsmith turned architect completed, after 16 years of work without scaffolding, a vast octagonal dome over the crossing of a century-old cathedral. The double-shelled design, assembled with four million bricks in a self-supporting herringbone pattern, spanned 42 metres — wider than any dome built since Roman antiquity. The cathedral had stood domeless for over a century, waiting for someone to figure out how.
events.revealBlurb: August 25, 1436 — consecrated. Filippo Brunelleschi at Santa Maria del Fiore, Florence. He refused to leave blueprints, fearing competitors would steal the ideas. Part of the technique was rediscovered only in the 20th century through forensic study of the bricks.

events.title: Machu Picchu Built
events.blurb: An Inca emperor's royal estate was built at 2,430 metres on a narrow mountain ridge above a river in the Andes, with 200 stone buildings — agricultural terraces, palaces, temples — arranged on a mountain site that seemed intended for dramatic rather than practical reasons. It was abandoned roughly a century later for unclear reasons, possibly connected to the Spanish conquest of the Inca. The site remained unknown to the Spanish and, largely, to the outside world until 1911.
events.revealBlurb: c. 1450 — emperor Pachacuti. The American explorer Hiram Bingham encountered it on July 24, 1911. Local farmers had never really forgotten it; the "rediscovery" was primarily for outside audiences. It is now one of the New Seven Wonders of the World.

events.title: US Capitol Cornerstone Laid
events.blurb: The president of the newly independent United States — wearing a Masonic apron — laid the cornerstone of a new federal capitol building on a wooded hill above the banks of the Potomac River. The building was meant to house the U.S. Congress. The winning design, by a Scottish-trained amateur architect, was a neoclassical rotunda crowned with a low dome; later architects would replace the dome with a much taller cast-iron one during the Civil War.
events.revealBlurb: September 18, 1793 — George Washington at Jenkins Hill (now Capitol Hill), Washington, D.C. Designer: William Thornton. The current wedding-cake dome was built 1855-1866 by Thomas U. Walter and crowned with the Statue of Freedom during the Civil War. Slave labour built much of the original building.

events.title: Statue of Liberty Dedicated
events.blurb: A 46-metre-tall copper statue of a robed woman holding a torch, a gift from the French people commemorating American independence (with an eye toward French republican aspirations), was dedicated on a small island in New York Harbor in the rain. It had been designed by a French sculptor, its internal iron framework engineered by the man who would five years later design a certain Paris tower, and shipped across the Atlantic in 350 pieces.
events.revealBlurb: October 28, 1886 — sculptor Frédéric Auguste Bartholdi; engineer Gustave Eiffel. The statue was meant to arrive for the 1876 centennial; it missed by a decade due to fundraising troubles. The poem on its pedestal ("Give me your tired, your poor...") was added in 1903 from a sonnet by Emma Lazarus.

events.title: Don Giovanni Premieres
events.blurb: A 31-year-old composer conducted the premiere of his two-act opera about a dissolute nobleman's pursuit of women and eventual descent into Hell, before Prague nobility at the Estates Theatre. According to his librettist, the overture was composed the night before the premiere while the composer's wife kept him awake through the small hours with punch and fairy tales.

events.title: The Rite of Spring Riot
events.blurb: A 30-year-old Russian composer's ballet score, depicting a pagan spring ritual with jagged rhythms, dissonant chord stacks, and primitivist choreography, premiered at a new Paris theatre and nearly caused a full-scale audience riot. Shouts, whistles, and fistfights broke out within minutes; the choreographer had to shout counts to dancers from the wings because they couldn't hear the orchestra. The piece is now considered one of the pivotal works of 20th-century music.
events.revealBlurb: May 29, 1913 — Igor Stravinsky and Ballets Russes at Théâtre des Champs-Élysées, Paris. Choreography by Vaslav Nijinsky. The Parisian critic Carl Van Vechten reported his seat-neighbour beating rhythmically on his head with his fists in distress.

events.title: Woodstock Festival Opens
events.blurb: A music festival on a dairy farm in upstate New York that had sold 186,000 advance tickets was overwhelmed by more than 400,000 attendees in the preceding 48 hours, forcing organisers to declare it a free event and abandon the ticket booths. Thirty-two acts performed over four rain-soaked days, and the festival became the defining cultural gathering of its generation.

events.title: Hip-Hop Born in the Bronx
events.blurb: An 18-year-old Jamaican-born DJ, using two turntables to extend the instrumental breaks of funk and soul records, played his younger sister's back-to-school party in the rec room of a public housing building in the South Bronx. His technique of looping drum breaks became the foundation of hip-hop. The party went so well that he began DJ-ing at local parks and block parties; rappers (then called MCs) began performing over his sets. A new culture was born.
events.revealBlurb: August 11, 1973 — DJ Kool Herc (Clive Campbell) at 1520 Sedgwick Avenue, the Bronx. The address is now a national historic site. Herc's "merry-go-round" technique of using two copies of the same record to loop the break is still the foundation of every hip-hop DJ set.

events.title: Tupac Shakur Killed
events.blurb: A 25-year-old rapper and actor, riding as a passenger in a black BMW along a Las Vegas strip intersection on a Saturday night after attending a championship boxing match, was shot four times from a white Cadillac that pulled up alongside. He survived six days in critical condition before dying in hospital. The murder has never been prosecuted; the lead suspect was killed in retaliation two years later.
events.revealBlurb: September 7, 1996 — Tupac was shot; died September 13. The concurrent East Coast-West Coast rap war, partly stoked by publicists, produced a second casualty six months later when the Notorious B.I.G. was killed in Los Angeles. In 2023, Duane "Keefe D" Davis was charged with Tupac's murder.

events.title: First Tour de France
events.blurb: A French sports newspaper, in an effort to increase circulation, organized a 2,428-kilometre bicycle race around the perimeter of France — six stages, each the length of an ultra-endurance event today, with sleep-deprived cyclists riding through the night on dirt roads with a single fixed gear. Sixty cyclists started; only 21 finished. A chimney sweep named Maurice Garin won the inaugural race over 19 days of riding.
events.revealBlurb: July 1-19, 1903 — organized by L'Auto magazine, a forerunner of L'Équipe. Garin's margin of victory was an implausible 2 hours 49 minutes. He was later stripped of his 1904 title for cheating (taking trains). The race continues annually with a couple of wartime interruptions.

events.title: Battle of the Sexes Tennis Match
events.blurb: A 29-year-old professional tennis player defeated a 55-year-old former Wimbledon champion in straight sets before a crowd of 30,000 at the Houston Astrodome and a television audience of 90 million. The retired player had publicly declared that no woman could defeat him, offering a $100,000 prize to any who tried.

events.title: The Rumble in the Jungle
events.blurb: A 32-year-old heavyweight boxing challenger, widely predicted to lose to the younger and vastly more powerful champion, leaned back against the ropes for seven rounds and absorbed punishing body blows — a tactic he later nicknamed "rope-a-dope." In the 8th, when the champion visibly tired, the challenger delivered a flurry of punches that knocked him out. The fight was held in an African capital as part of a pioneering pan-African promotion.
events.revealBlurb: October 30, 1974 — Muhammad Ali KO'd George Foreman at the Stade du 20 Mai in Kinshasa, Zaire (now Democratic Republic of the Congo). Promoter Don King organized it. The event was immortalized in the 1996 documentary "When We Were Kings."

events.title: Cubs Win World Series
events.blurb: The Chicago Cubs won their first World Series championship in 108 years, defeating the Cleveland Indians in a 10-inning seventh game interrupted by a rain delay. The Cubs' championship drought — dating back to 1908 — was the longest in American professional sports. Their 1945 loss had been attributed by fans to the "Curse of the Billy Goat," thrown at the owner of a neighbourhood tavern who had been asked to remove his pet goat from a World Series game.
events.revealBlurb: November 2-3, 2016 — Cubs 8, Indians 7 in 10 innings at Progressive Field, Cleveland. The game ended at 12:47 AM local time on November 3. Cubs manager Joe Maddon, third baseman Kris Bryant, and first baseman Anthony Rizzo led the championship team. Chicago celebrated with a victory parade of 5 million people.

events.title: Messi Wins World Cup
events.blurb: A 35-year-old Argentine forward, in his fifth and final World Cup tournament, led his team to a 3-3 draw against France in the final, then won a penalty shootout 4-2 at a Qatari stadium. He scored two of the final's goals himself, then converted his penalty. The tournament's signature absence from his glittering career — the World Cup — was at last his. It was widely described as the greatest World Cup final ever played.
events.revealBlurb: December 18, 2022 — Argentina 3-3 France (4-2 pens), Lusail Stadium, Qatar. Messi and Kylian Mbappé combined for six goals between them. Messi had already won seven Ballon d'Or awards, a record; he would win an eighth in 2023. Mbappé became the first to score a hat-trick in a World Cup final since Geoff Hurst in 1966.

events.title: Sistine Chapel Ceiling Unveiled
events.blurb: A 37-year-old Florentine sculptor, who had accepted a papal commission reluctantly after four years insisting he was not a painter, unveiled 500 square metres of freshly painted fresco covering the ceiling of a Vatican chapel. The work, which had taken four years, depicted nine scenes from Genesis surrounded by 300 figures. The artist had painted it while standing, not lying down as myth claims, his neck bent back for hours daily.
events.revealBlurb: October 31, 1512 — Michelangelo Buonarroti. He wrote a sonnet complaining of his neck: "I've grown a goiter by dwelling in this den… my beard turns up to heaven." Restoration between 1980 and 1994 revealed vivid colours under 400 years of candle smoke.

events.title: Luther Posts the 95 Theses
events.blurb: A 33-year-old German university theologian sent his local archbishop a letter enclosing a 95-point list of academic propositions challenging the papal indulgence system — the practice of selling forgiveness of sins. By tradition, he also posted the Latin theses on the door of his university church, which served as a community bulletin board. Copies reached print within weeks and spread across Germany. He had intended academic debate; he ignited the Protestant Reformation.
events.revealBlurb: October 31, 1517 — Martin Luther at Wittenberg Castle Church. Most scholars doubt the physical nailing-to-the-door story; the letter to Archbishop Albrecht of Mainz is well-documented. October 31 is now celebrated as Reformation Day in many Protestant countries.

events.title: Cortés Reaches Tenochtitlán
events.blurb: A 34-year-old Spanish conquistador, in defiance of orders from the governor of Cuba who had tried to recall him, entered the causeway-linked lakeside capital of the Aztec Triple Alliance — a city of perhaps 200,000 people, one of the largest in the world, built on an island in a high-altitude lake. The Aztec emperor met him with courtesy, gifts, and quiet suspicion. Within two years the emperor would be dead and the city in ruins.
events.revealBlurb: November 8, 1519 — Hernán Cortés meets Moctezuma II in Tenochtitlán (modern Mexico City). The Spanish force was about 500 strong, augmented by thousands of Tlaxcalan allies who hated the Aztecs. Cortés had burned his own ships on the coast to prevent desertion.

events.title: Globe Theatre Opens
events.blurb: A London acting company, evicted from their original playhouse when their landlord refused to renew the lease, dismantled the building overnight, carried the timbers across the frozen Thames, and rebuilt them into a new circular theatre on the south bank. Their principal playwright and shareholder produced several of his greatest plays on its stage over the next 14 years, until a cannon effect during a performance of Henry VIII set the thatched roof alight.
events.revealBlurb: 1599 — the Lord Chamberlain's Men; William Shakespeare was a shareholder. It burned on June 29, 1613; was rebuilt; was demolished in 1644 under Puritan hostility to theatre. A faithful replica opened in 1997 near the original site.

events.title: Jamestown Colony Founded
events.blurb: English settlers dispatched by the Virginia Company came ashore on a low, marshy peninsula in the tidewater and drove stakes for the first permanent English settlement in the territory that would become the United States. Of the roughly 104 men and boys who arrived, fewer than 40 survived their first year, undone by brackish drinking water, starvation, and disease.
events.revealBlurb: May 14, 1607 — Virginia. The site was chosen partly because its deep water let ships dock without anchors — and partly because it looked easy to defend. It was also mosquito-ridden and had no fresh water. Within nine months, roughly 65% of the colonists were dead.
